strengths: The paper proposes a novel and potentially useful geometry-grounded analogue of byte-pair encoding, combining hierarchical motif merging, medoid-based quantization, and inverse-kinematics refinement.
The method produces variable-length, multiresolution structural tokens represented by observed fragments, offering better intrinsic interpretability than latent vector codebooks.

The paper examines several relevant dimensions—compression and reconstruction, held-out datasets, downstream prediction, token utilization, generation, and qualitative interpretation—and provides extensive pseudocode and hyperparameter documentation.
The glue-optimization ablation provides concrete evidence that global geometric correction materially improves reconstruction fidelity.
weaknesses: The downstream evaluation does not isolate the tokenizer's contribution. GEOBPE combines ESM3 features with a trainable bidirectional Tree-LSTM, while the reported ESM3 baseline apparently lacks this additional architecture. Controls using the same encoder with random, balanced, or alternative trees are essential; without them, the large gains cannot be attributed to the learned vocabulary or hierarchy.

The interpretability evaluation is structurally biased. For every annotated domain, it searches over all consecutive unions of predicted segments and selects the union maximizing IoU. Any sufficiently fine partition can approximate arbitrary interval annotations under this protocol, so near-perfect scores do not establish that individual GEOBPE tokens correspond to functional domains. Comparisons with other tokenizers or segmentation algorithms are also absent.

The expert case studies are anecdotal and apparently selected post hoc. They invoke aromatic residues, polar interactions, and side-chain chemistry even though GEOBPE encodes neither sequence nor side chains. No blinded protocol, selection procedure, expert credentials, inter-rater agreement, or counterexamples are reported.

The generative evidence is weak and overstated: only 100 samples are evaluated, GEOBPE achieves merely 3–4% designability, and differences of a few successful samples are presented without uncertainty or repeated training runs. The text's characterization of the outputs as '99% unique and designable' conflates roughly 99% uniqueness with only 4% designability.

Several headline comparisons are not like-for-like. The tokenizer sizes, training sets, architectures, and training-data scales differ substantially, while the claimed compression advantages accompany sizable reconstruction degradation. The manuscript therefore does not convincingly establish superiority at matched distortion or under matched resource conditions.

The experiments provide no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests for randomized k-medoids, downstream learning, or language-model training. Important implementation details for the downstream models and the exact accounting of tokenizer-description cost in BPR are also insufficiently clear.

Some central claims exceed the evidence: the abstract's test/train distortion ratio of 1.0–1.1 conflicts with the 1.16–1.28 values stated later; performance is not consistently best across tasks; and the results do not justify claims of functional meaning, evolutionary grounding, or a foundation for structure-native language models.

strengths: The geometry-grounded BPE formulation is an interesting and potentially useful alternative to fixed-resolution vector-quantized protein structure tokenizers. Combining hierarchical medoid motifs with inverse-kinematics correction is technically motivated.

The paper examines several relevant dimensions—reconstruction, compression, held-out generalization, vocabulary utilization, downstream prediction, and generation—and includes a useful ablation showing that glue optimization substantially improves reconstruction.

The appendices provide extensive pseudocode, dataset descriptions, complexity analysis, and some implementation details. The reported reconstruction/compression tradeoff appears promising enough to merit further investigation.
weaknesses: The downstream evaluation does not isolate the contribution of the tokenizer. GEOBPE uses pretrained ESM3 features followed by a learned bidirectional TreeLSTM over its hierarchy, whereas competing tokenizers use their native representations. Essential controls such as ESM3 with a parameter-matched sequential model, random or balanced merge trees, alternative pooling hierarchies, and residue-level features without GEOBPE are absent. The unchanged performance when training GEOBPE on only 1% of the structures is also consistent with ESM3 and the downstream architecture driving the results.

Several central claims materially overstate the tables. GEOBPE does not consistently outperform leading tokenizers across all reported splits, and continuous baselines substantially outperform it on average for flexibility prediction. Its generation results are weak: mean scTM is at most 0.277 and only 3–4% of samples are designable, despite language suggesting that generated structures are broadly designable. Comparisons against strong contemporary backbone generators are missing.

The interpretability evaluation is not convincing. For each annotated domain, the metric selects the best consecutive union of predicted segments; any sufficiently fine contiguous partition can approximate an arbitrary interval nearly perfectly. Consequently, the approximately 0.99 scores can arise from segment granularity rather than meaningful token-domain correspondence. The random equal-length partition baseline does not adequately control for the actual segment-length distribution or hierarchy. The claimed expert evaluation consists of a few unblinded, post-hoc narratives with no expert-selection protocol, independent ratings, controls, or inter-rater agreement.

Compression accounting is insufficiently transparent. Although the definition includes the description length of the tokenizer, the experiments do not clearly specify how the large medoid vocabulary, merge keys/tree, glue-angle symbols, encoder, and decoder are serialized and charged. Exact BPR values and accounting components are not tabulated. This makes the headline order-of-magnitude compression comparisons difficult to audit and potentially not apples-to-apples.

The empirical Pareto-optimality and OOD claims are based on a limited collection of configurations and baselines, with methods trained on dramatically different corpus sizes. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity analyses for the stochastic k-medoids initialization. Ratios of test to training RMSD alone do not establish superior OOD generalization when absolute distortions and data distributions differ.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the long pseudocode appendix. The manuscript's code-availability link is empty, and important settings for tokenizer optimization and downstream models are not fully reported. There are also consequential notation inconsistencies in the glue variables and indices—for example, phi versus phi at the next residue and an apparent substitution of psi for omega in the global glue algorithm.

Overall, the core tokenizer idea may be worthwhile, but the evidence does not substantiate the strongest claims about representation quality, interpretability, generation, or compression. Corrected evaluations and stronger controls would require substantial new experimental work rather than a minor revision.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/1aad5e5c29ee4fb69470d615d7967111/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents an original and compelling geometry-grounded analogue of byte-pair encoding, producing variable-length motifs and explicit merge hierarchies rather than fixed-size latent codes.

The combination of medoid-based motif quantization and inverse-kinematics glue optimization is technically interesting and well motivated; the glue-removal ablation shows a substantial RMSD degradation from 1.66 to 4.39, supporting this design choice.

The paper studies an unusually broad set of properties, including compression-distortion behavior, held-out reconstruction, vocabulary utilization, downstream transfer, generation, and interpretability.
The adaptive vocabulary exposes a useful, smooth compression-distortion tradeoff, while the medoid prototypes provide a more concrete geometric interpretation than learned latent vectors.

The manuscript includes extensive pseudocode, complexity analysis, hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and data-efficiency ablations. The reported performance with only 1% of the tokenizer-training data is promising.
weaknesses: The downstream comparison does not isolate the benefit of GEOBPE. GEOBPE applies a trainable up-down TreeLSTM to pretrained ESM3 features, whereas competing tokenizers use their own representations. Essential parameter-matched controls—such as the same encoder with random, balanced, or sequence-based trees—are absent, so gains cannot confidently be attributed to the learned vocabulary or hierarchy.

The functional-interpretability evaluation is structurally biased toward very high scores: each annotated contiguous domain is matched to its best consecutive union of predicted segments. Any sufficiently fine contiguous partition can approximate a domain under this protocol, as also suggested by the already high random-partition baselines. Consequently, the near-perfect F1 and IoU values do not establish meaningful functional alignment.

The qualitative interpretations invoke aromatic cages, charged residues, hydrogen bonds, and other side-chain chemistry even though GEOBPE encodes only backbone geometry and explicitly omits sequence and side chains. These examples therefore provide weak evidence that the tokens themselves carry the claimed biochemical semantics.

The generative evidence is only a limited proof of concept: mean scTM is at most 0.277 and only 3–4% of samples exceed the designability threshold, based on 100 samples and weak tokenizer baselines. The main-text phrasing about '99% unique and designable backbones' is misleading because approximately 99% are unique, not designable.

The central BPR comparison is insufficiently reproducible and may not be apples-to-apples. Although the definition includes tokenizer description length, the paper does not explain how variable-length medoid coordinates, glue quantizers, mappings, or neural baseline parameters are serialized and charged. No uncertainty estimates are reported for randomized k-medoids or downstream experiments.

There are specification inconsistencies—for example, the glue variables alternate between omega and psi in the notation and algorithms—and no explicit unseen-structure encoding algorithm. The code URL is also blank in the submitted manuscript. These issues impede verification of an otherwise detailed method.

Overall, the core idea is promising and potentially publishable, but the evidence for the strongest transfer and interpretability claims is not sufficiently controlled for acceptance at this threshold.

strengths: Introduces a novel and technically interesting geometric analogue of byte-pair encoding, combining hierarchical motif merging, medoid-based quantization, and inverse-kinematics refinement.
The method produces variable-length, multi-resolution structural tokens and explicit merge hierarchies, offering capabilities that fixed-resolution VQ-VAE tokenizers do not naturally provide.

The paper is unusually broad experimentally, covering reconstruction, compression, out-of-distribution behavior, vocabulary utilization, downstream prediction, generation, scalability, and interpretability; the glue-optimization ablation provides particularly clear evidence for an important design component.
Results indicate promising reconstruction/compression trade-offs, strong generalization to CAMEO and CASP14, and practical tokenization of a substantially larger AlphaFold-derived corpus.
The manuscript provides extensive algorithmic pseudocode, complexity discussion, hyperparameter documentation, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The downstream-transfer comparison does not isolate the claimed benefit of the learned GEOBPE vocabulary. GEOBPE-TRANSFER adds a hierarchical propagation architecture on top of pretrained ESM3 features, whereas competing tokenizers use their native encoder representations. Essential controls—ESM3 with the same tree architecture but random, frequency-based, or generic geometric hierarchies—are missing, so the sizable gains cannot be attributed specifically to GEOBPE tokens.

The compression comparison is difficult to interpret fairly. BPR amortizes tokenizer description length over the evaluated corpus, strongly penalizing large neural tokenizers such as ESM3 and ProToken, but the manuscript does not clearly document how every model parameter, variable-length prototype, glue quantizer, hierarchy, and numerical precision is encoded. The resulting headline compression ratios may therefore reflect accounting and corpus-size choices rather than an intrinsic coding advantage.

The interpretability evidence is weaker than claimed. CATH agreement uses a best consecutive block of predicted segments for each domain, which makes recall nearly trivial and allows multiple tokens to explain one annotation; there are no comparisons against other structure tokenizers or standard domain-segmentation methods. The three expert case studies are anecdotal and apparently unblinded, and some functional explanations rely on side-chain chemistry even though GEOBPE itself excludes side chains.

The generative evaluation is small and not fully controlled: only 100 samples are used, uncertainty is not reported, the GEOBPE and VQ-VAE pipelines differ in decoding and validity constraints, and the larger-scale result is not compared under matched data and model capacity against strong modern backbone generators. It supports feasibility more than the broad language-modeling claims.

Statistical uncertainty and repeated-run variability are absent across most downstream, reconstruction, and generation experiments. The paper often interprets small differences as meaningful despite no confidence intervals or significance tests.

Several central claims are overstated: the method is described as architecture-agnostic without evidence beyond one ESM3-based transfer pipeline, functional meaning is inferred primarily from boundary overlap and qualitative inspection, and “state-of-the-art” conclusions span settings with materially different training data, model capacity, and objectives. Overall, the core idea is promising, but controlled baselines and clearer rate accounting are needed before the main empirical conclusions are sufficiently convincing for acceptance.

strengths: The geometry-grounded analogue of BPE is an interesting and potentially useful idea: variable-length motif tokens, a merge hierarchy, medoid prototypes, and inverse-kinematics correction form a distinctive alternative to fixed-resolution VQ-VAE tokenizers.

The manuscript is ambitious and broad, covering reconstruction, out-of-distribution tokenization, downstream transfer, language modeling, scalability, and interpretability. The reported reconstruction results suggest a useful adjustable compression-distortion tradeoff.

The glue-optimization ablation provides concrete evidence that global geometric correction is important, and the 550K-structure tokenization experiment helps establish practical scalability at inference time.
The appendices contain extensive pseudocode, complexity discussion, hyperparameter documentation, and dataset descriptions, which are valuable foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The downstream comparison does not isolate the tokenizer's contribution. GEOBPE-TRANSFER combines ESM3 features with a trainable bidirectional TreeLSTM over the learned hierarchy, whereas competing rows use different encoders and representation pipelines. Crucial controlled baselines—such as the same ESM3 features and TreeLSTM with random, balanced, sequence-based, or alternative structural hierarchies—are absent. Consequently, the large gains cannot be attributed specifically to GEOBPE tokens or vocabulary.

The central interpretability evaluation is structurally biased. For every annotated domain, it selects the best arbitrary consecutive union of predicted segments. Since every segmentation partitions the entire chain, sufficiently many adjacent segments can approximate almost any domain interval. This explains why even random partitions attain very high scores and makes the near-perfect recall/F1/IoU weak evidence of biological alignment. Direct boundary metrics, matched-segment evaluations, and comparisons with established segmentation methods are needed.

The qualitative 'expert' evidence is not a credible expert study: only three examples are discussed, with no blinded protocol, number or qualifications of raters, independent annotations, or inter-rater agreement. Several interpretations invoke side-chain chemistry even though GEOBPE uses neither sequence nor side-chain information. The manuscript also inconsistently labels this analysis as PFAM agreement while using CATH FunFams.

The compression claims are insufficiently specified for a fair Pareto comparison. Although BPR includes the description length of the tokenizer, the paper does not state how medoid coordinates, quantizers, merge rules, floating-point precision, and decoders are encoded into L(T). The resulting BPR values and the claimed 10x advantage therefore cannot be independently verified or confidently compared across radically different tokenizer families.

The generative evidence is overstated. In the controlled 7.3M-model experiment, GEOBPE designability is only 3–4%, despite prose claiming '99% unique and designable' backbones; 99% is uniqueness, not designability. The larger experiment uses only 100 samples and compares its 21% designability with literature numbers under a different data/model regime, without uncertainty estimates or controlled contemporary baselines.

There are material inconsistencies in the geometric specification. The glue variables are alternately defined using (theta_CNCA, phi_i, omega_i), (theta_CNCA, omega_i, phi_{i+1}), and in Algorithm 12 (theta_CNCA, psi_i, phi_{i+1}); Algorithm 18 also stores omega and phi inside residue prototypes while other sections treat them as boundary glues. These discrepancies make the claimed encoder/decoder and inverse-kinematics procedure ambiguous and could affect correctness.

Most empirical results report single point estimates despite random k-medoids initialization, data subsampling, neural training, and generation. There are no multi-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the main reconstruction, downstream, and generative comparisons.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive pseudocode: the promised code link is blank, several implementation choices are deferred to another work, and exact downstream model/training details are insufficient to reconstruct the strongest results. Overall, the core idea has promise, but the principal transfer, interpretability, compression, and generation claims are not supported rigorously enough for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: GEOBPE is a novel and well-motivated geometric analogue of byte-pair encoding: it learns variable-length hierarchical backbone motifs while using differentiable inverse kinematics to control accumulated reconstruction drift.

The paper provides substantial empirical evidence across reconstruction, compression, OOD generalization, downstream transfer, token utilization, and unconditional generation. The compression–distortion curves and evaluation on CAMEO/CASP14 are particularly useful.

The hierarchical vocabulary is practically meaningful: it supports adjustable resolution, architecture-independent feature aggregation, and direct autoregressive modeling without a learned neural decoder.

Ablations cover important design choices, including glue optimization, training-set size, vocabulary resolution, clustering limits, loss weights, and quantization settings. The glue-optimization ablation shows a clear and substantial effect.

The manuscript is unusually thorough about algorithms, computational complexity, hyperparameters, runtime, scaling behavior, and limitations, which should aid reproducibility. weaknesses: The downstream gains are not cleanly attributable to the tokenizer. GEOBPE-TRANSFER combines ESM3 features with a learned up–down TreeLSTM, whereas several baselines use their native representations. Essential controls include the same TreeLSTM over random, balanced, sequential, or alternative hierarchies and matched parameter/optimization budgets.

The functional-interpretability evidence is substantially overstated. Because predicted motifs partition the entire chain and the metric selects the best consecutive block of motifs for each domain, sufficiently short segments can approximate almost any interval. Even random partitions obtain high domain-level scores, so near-perfect recall and IoU do not by themselves establish functional alignment.

The expert case studies are anecdotal and lack a documented blinded evaluation protocol, number and qualifications of experts, inter-rater agreement, or negative controls. Some functional interpretations rely on side-chain chemistry even though GEOBPE tokenization uses only backbone geometry.

Compression comparisons require clearer accounting. Although BPR formally includes tokenizer description length, the manuscript does not make sufficiently explicit how floating-point prototypes, glue quantizers, encoders/decoders, and precision are serialized consistently across methods. Baselines also differ greatly in training data and objectives.

The language-modeling evidence remains preliminary: the default model produces only 3–4% designable structures, and the scaled result changes data size, model size, and evaluation-length protocol simultaneously. Comparisons with prior generators are therefore not controlled enough to support strong generative claims.

Some algorithmic notation is internally inconsistent, particularly the definitions/indexing of glue angles across the main text and Algorithms 12, 19, and 20. The paper would benefit from a careful correctness pass and a single explicit end-to-end encoding/decoding specification.

Results are generally reported as point estimates without variation across tokenizer initialization, downstream training seeds, or generation runs, making it difficult to assess whether smaller differences are reliable.
